The June lecture from the cycle Anarchocapitalism will again be on an economic topic; we'll discuss what politicians do wrong, but also why - not every economic "mistake" is a serious mistake - it's often a cheap way to score political points that someone else will pay for. Unfortunately, politicians are also supported by some libertarian economists when they need to be relevant to government; I'm happy when they advise the government instead of the socialists, but on the other hand, unfortunately, it also has the opposite effect. I would like to talk about the economic mistakes that occur in democracies without regard to specific policies; I want to show it with specific examples, quite possibly we will also touch on something current (depending on the state of Hormuz). I will try to provide a counterweight to the views commonly presented in the (mainly public) media; we will deal with price and margin ceilings, but also people's favorite pastime - finding the "culprits" of high prices and making uninformed judgments about "fairness".

The eighth speaker of the "Freeport Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Karel Šindelář with his lecture "Freedom without a center: mind, nature and being".

Freedom can turn into a distant ideal, that the very idea of "one day I will be free" can create distance, desire, fear and the need for security - that is, mechanisms that paradoxically move us away from freedom. The same can also be a consequence of trying to define freedom firmly: Every definition creates a center, an authority or an arbiter. On the contrary, even one's own mind can be decentralized, similar to society. It is possible to release the inner "central authority" that evaluates, controls and directs. Indeed, the greatest lack of freedom can be rooted in our internal mechanisms of fear rather than in states and institutions. However, one can walk freely even in the midst of restrictions – much like the landscape, which is not the enemy but the environment. The lecture is not meant to bring ready-made answers, but to offer a common space for questioning our certainties, ideas and need for control.

Karel has long been devoted to contemplative practice and the themes of fear, death, love, life and freedom. He has been living a nomadic lifestyle for six years with his wife, three children and a dog. Although this was not always the case, today they do not feel part of any school of thought, ideology, movement or state. More than creating new definitions, he is interested in direct experience and observation - what can actually be experienced, not just named.

The fourth speaker of the "2026 Freeport Conference: Freedom Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "Anarchoagorism: A Practical Path to Freedom".

Libertarians (especially anarcho-capitalists) understand that (and why) central planning doesn't work; however, this often does not prevent them from thinking of freedom as something that can be centrally planned - they desire to live more freely so much that as a result they fall into the same trap as statists, when they are too eager to believe that the answer to their needs can come "from above". However, we cannot talk our way into freedom; nor can it be imposed on anyone who is not interested in it - not only does the end justify the means, but centrally controlled decentralization doesn't even make sense, it's an oxymoron. What about that? The answer comes from anarchoagorism – by creating agoras (islands of freedom based on voluntariness and spontaneous order), disobedient individuals can locally shield the power of external authorities; the goal is not to defeat or dominate the state, but to exist in parallel independently of it.

The first speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Jan "Blue Bird" Čmolík with his lecture "Murray Newton Rothbard - intellectual background and the concept of the social contract".

The fruits of the work of Murray Newton Rothbard - the "spiritual father" of anarcho-capitalism - we all know and reap to some extent in the Freeport Channel; however, let's also look at its roots and explore the intellectual background from which it originates.

Jan Čmolík works as a self-employed person in the role of interim manager, focusing on the restructuring of commercial companies. In his practice, he focuses on optimizing processes and eliminating redundant or duplicate activities that do not bring added value. He gained experience in a wide range of fields – from the textile, chemical and food industry, to engineering and metallurgy to the field of transport. In addition to his professional activity, he has long been concerned with the relationship between the ideas formulated by the classics of economics and the reality we live in today. He is the author of Economic Irregulars - an abridged history of economic thought, which he published under the pseudonym Blue Bird. He perceives the topic of freedom as key. People often live in the belief that those who do nothing wrong have nothing to fear - but the reality is different; in severely totalitarian regimes, this is not the case, but even in our democracy, this is not the case - or rather, it may be the case most of the time, but you never know when you will find yourself in the wrong place at the wrong time. A person does not have to be a criminal or harm anyone to be occasionally affected by the weight of state power; I think it's good to be prepared. From October, the Anarcho-Capitalism cycle shifts again; this time to the emerging libertarian den Liberty Loft. In order to maintain a balance between the topics of personal and economic freedom, I would like to focus on capitalism this time; the latter is the target of criticism by many, often including anarchists, while everyone criticizes him for something different - from excessive hierarchization and centralization to the destruction of the environment to insufficient interest in the soul of the individual. I myself could identify with some points of this criticism, but I would not blame capitalism per se for any of them; because I am convinced that this system only reflects the needs and nature of people in society (both on the side of consumers and producers), while it does not create the problems described above in itself, it only brings them to light. So let's discuss it more closely together!

The state is criticized from all sides – as dysfunctional, inefficient, unjust, authoritarian or blind to the needs of minorities. But what if all these complaints are not just random complaints, but a symptom of a deeper flaw in the way the state works as a process? In this lecture, we will look at specific problems that people of different value frameworks feel: from the alienation of the majority to the failure of the rule of law to the oppression of minorities. For each point, we will focus not only on its symptoms, but above all on where the very mechanism that should solve these problems fails. And we will also propose specific alternatives – small but significant interventions that could correct these defects.

I'm going to talk about anarchoagorism, which is making more and more sense to me; it differs from anarcho-capitalism in that it doesn't recognize political solutions, which resonates with me quite a bit, although I probably wouldn't be as sharp about it. title: Urza and Lawrence "Larry" Reed on freedom and humanity
desc:
If you enjoyed the lecture and found it valuable, please consider sending a donation!
Regular donations or LN: https://opristavu.urza.cz/

IBAN: CZ72 2010 0000 0022 0135 9764
--------
Larry captivated me with his talk at LibertyCon; it was undoubtedly the best lecture of the event for me and perhaps one of the best I've ever heard. That's why I was delighted when he accepted my invitation to appear in the Free Haven.
We discussed his concept of human virtues as the foundation of liberty. I described my concept of outer freedom and inner freedom (limited by fear) — an idea Larry resonated with. We concluded by discussing how to practically cultivate these virtues in everyday life.
--------
Biographies I Recommend — by Lawrence W. Reed:
1/ Beneath a Scarlet Sky by Mark Sullivan—the story of World War II Italian resistance figure Pino Lella, who is still living today at 92.
2/ Bonhoeffer: Pastor, Martyr, Prophet, Spy by Eric Metaxas—about Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the Lutheran pastor who became a part of the 1944 plot to kill Adolf Hitler.  
3/ Destiny of the Republic: A Tale of Madness, Medicine and the Murder of a President by Candace Millard—follows the final two years in the lives of James A. Garfield, 20th U.S. President, and his assassin, Charles Guiteau.
4/ Longitude: The Story of a Lone Genius Who Solved the Greatest Scientific Problem of His Time by Dava Sobel—about how the clockmaker John Harrison won the prize for discovering how to determine longitude at sea.
5/ Ronald Reagan: How an Ordinary Man Became an Extraordinary Leader by Dinesh D'Souza—one of the best of many Reagan biographies.
6/ When Character Was King by Peggy Noonan—another great and inspiring Reagan biography.
7/ Bury the Chains: Prophets and Rebels in the Fight to Free an Empire's Slaves by Adam Hochschild—an excellent history of the British anti-slavery campaign, with special focus on the personalities of Thomas Clarkson and Olaudah Equiano.
8/ Amazing Grace by Eric Metaxas—the best biography of anti-slavery parliamentarian William Wilberforce.
9/ The Myth of the Robber Barons by Burton W. Folsom—excellent chapters on American business figures such as Cornelius Vanderbilt, John D. Rockefeller, Charles Schwab and others.
10/ Real Heroes: Inspiring True Stories of Courage, Character and Conviction by Lawrence W. Reed—contains 40 chapters on great men and women of politics, business, humanitarianism, etc.
11/ The Cross and the Switchblade by David Wilkerson—the story of a Pennsylvania preacher who attempts to change lives in inner city New York.
12/ Cicero by Anthony Everitt—the best biography of the ancient Roman statesman and orator.
13/ The Last Jeffersonian: Grover Cleveland and the Path to Restoring the Republic by Ryan S. Walters—about one of America's greatest but forgotten Presidents.
14/ Margaret Thatcher: Everything She Wants by Charles Moore—focuses on the Iron Lady's premiership from the Falklands War on.
15/ Sophie Scholl and the White Rose by Annette Dumbach and Jud Newborn—fascinating story of a brave college student who challenged the Nazi regime.
16/ The Final Race: The Incredible World War II Story of the Olympian Who Inspired Chariots of Fire by Eric T. Eichinger and Eva Marie Everson – about Scottish athlete and missionary Eric Liddell, a man who was about as good as it gets.
17/ A Man of Iron: The Turbulent Life and Improbable Presidency of Grover Cleveland by Troy Senik – America's 22nd and 24th president stood for sound money, free enterprise, low taxes and strong character.
18/ The Child is Father of the Man: C. H. Spurgeon by Tom Nettles – one of several good biographies of the most famous minister of 19th Century England.
19/ The Revolutionary: Samuel Adams by Stacy Schiff—a thorough recounting of the man and his principles that played a huge role in the founding of America.
20/ Red Scarf Girl: A Memoir of the Cultural Revolution by Ji-Li Jiang—a story of the horrors of Mao Zedong's murderous regime from one who experienced the worst of it.
21/ Founding Martyr: The Life and Death of Dr. Joseph Warren, the American Revolution's Lost Hero by Christian Di Spigna—a thrilling walk through the beginnings of the American Revolution and the story of a courageous man who gave his life for it at Bunker Hill.
22/ The Jazz Age President: Warren Harding by Ryan Walters—America's 29th president, often derided as among our worst, deserves far more appreciation than he gets, and Walters explains why.

– Lawrence “Lary” Reed; libertarian; free man; president emeritus of the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE)
– Urza (www.urza.cz); author of Anarchocapitalism; creator of Freeport; co-founder and head of the Ludwig von Mises Institute; member of the Freedom of Learning board; a teacher at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage

One lecture at the Cherubín teahouse eventually became a whole series; I like to go back there because the place has the right tea tree and a great atmosphere (and a Buddha statue with the inscription: "When the god said: "Let there be light," the sound already existed.").
I consider the principle of non-aggression to be one of the basic pillars of anarcho-capitalism; polycentric law is then a practical implementation of free market law. How are they related? The April lecture in the Anarcho-Capitalism series will take place the day after April Fools' Day, which is a good thing, because otherwise you might think I'm joking; I want to calculate how much the state actually costs us. Being a theorist (which many consider a slur, but I certainly am not), you are used to theory from me; this time, however, we will look at the specific practice of the state - we will calculate not only individual taxes (including those called "insurance", fees and the like), but also other costs. We will pay special attention to pensions, as they make up the largest part of the state budget; and we will show how we could live without a pay-as-you-go - Ponzi - pension system. I will also explain why the day of tax freedom according to the Freeport would be even after the Deloitte or Liberal.

I want to dedicate the March lecture from the series Anarchocapitalism to a topic I have been dealing with for almost twenty years; that theme is spontaneous order - the creation of rules "from below" without the existence of a central authority or violent coercion. After studying theory for so long, there is nothing better than when one gets the opportunity to verify one's knowledge in practice! In Hedgehog Without a Cage, I understood that schools based on self-directed education are excellent examples of decentralized rule-making; so I started visiting these schools and comparing the experience from Ježek with other similar collectives. In doing so, I came to some unexpected conclusions that really surprised me; and it is in this lecture that I would very much like to share them with you and also discuss them.

The fourth speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2025: Culture Wars Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Vláďa Krupa with his lecture "History of Culture Wars".

Political agitation since the mass expansion of suffrage takes place not only through direct methods such as election campaigns or advertising spots, but also through indirect influences that have a long-term and often subtle impact on public opinion. These indirect methods are, for example, novels, songs, plays, films and other forms of mass-consumed culture. These cultural influences often shape the political opinions of people who shy away from direct political messages. An example of the influence of these cultural methods is the process that took place in Great Britain in the 19th century. There, a combination of literary influences and the programs of the Fabian Society succeeded in transforming the ethos of classical liberalism into evolutionary socialism. Key figures of this change were, for example, John Stuart Mill, Bernard Shaw, Sidney Webb or authors such as Carlyle, Ruskin and Kingsley. This process of transformation of public opinion from the perception of state power as an inhibiting factor of progress to the perception of the state as a guarantee of freedom and an engine of progress was achieved to a large extent precisely through the non-violent path of cultural influences.

Vladimír Krupa is the co-founder of the Czech Mises Institute, an organization focused on spreading the ideas of the Austrian school of economics and individual freedom. As a prominent translator and author of articles, he has been devoted to the topics of economic history and monetary history for a long time, which enables him to look at the culture wars from a unique economic and historical angle.

The third speaker of the "2025 Freeport Conference: Culture Wars Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "Culture Wars or Freedom?".

Conservatives feel that progressive "woke" propaganda is taking away their freedom (often through the state); progressives, on the other hand, are convinced that their freedom is limited precisely by conservatives (often through state intervention). And so culture wars arise... But which of the above statements is true? Unfortunately, both; and when two fight, the third laughs. Who is the third one? The state, of course... What about it? I'm afraid the only workable solution is to stop fighting, however tempting it may be to involve the state in the conflict; for the state is a bad servant, but a bad master. I find it infinitely naive to think that the culture war can be "won" with the help of state power without serious consequences for both sides; thus only authoritarians can win, while freethinkers will be defeated.

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author and teacher at the self-governing Hedgehog Without a Cage school; wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. For fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, education, the free market and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, discusses, debates and makes videos. Together with his student Emma from the Hedgehog without a cage, he forms the Free Harbor; he heads the Czech and Slovak Institute of Ludwig von Mises, of which he is a co-founder; belongs to the board of the Freedom of Learning association and cooperates with many libertarian initiatives. You can find more about him on the Urza.cz website.

The second speaker of the "2025 Freeport Conference: Culture Wars Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Tim Kožuchov with his lecture "Let's not be afraid of progressivism".

Most people associate the word progress with a positive emotion. But why is this not the case when we talk about progressivism as a political ideology? During the lecture, we will talk about the history and meaning of this term. We will look at a frequent dispute in libertarian circles about whether a free society must also be a progressive society. Progressivism does not have to be about imposing new values, but about opening space for dialogue and respect for diversity.

The lecture will be given by Timofej Kožuchov. Tim was born in Russia, has Czech citizenship. He studied political science, economics and philosophy in London. On his channel Debatní deník, he comments on social issues and debates with people he disagrees with. In 2022, then a staunch socialist, he first debated with Urza about ankap and freedom. After reading many books and listening to many lectures, Tim is now a libertarian.

The first speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2025: Culture wars yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Roman Joch with his lecture "Why conservatism is for freedom and why progressivism is against it".

Conservatism wants the state to defend society, but not to interfere with its spontaneous, free development; progressivism wants the state to intervene and "improve" it, prohibiting and commanding people to do various things. Conservatism is for private property, progressivism not so much, or even against. Conservatism perceives man as a unique individual, an original; progressivism through the prism of gender, racial, sexual, cis- or trans-gender identity and intersectionality. Conservatism wants to protect (conserve) Western Civilization, the cradle of freedom; progressivism considers it uniquely evil and wants to "deconstruct" it and replace it with a new, "better" post-civilization.

Roman Joch (1971) is a columnist and university teacher. He studied general medicine at Charles University in Prague. He is the chairman of the Civic Institute. In the years 2010-12, he was an advisor to the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic for human rights and foreign policy, and in the years 2020-23, he was the director of the Institute for Work and Family Research in Bratislava, Slovakia. He is a teacher at the University of Economics and CEVRO University, where he also works as a Senior Fellow of its Center for Transatlantic Relations (PCTR). He is the author of several books and studies on political philosophy and politics, a contributor to the Czech and Slovak media. Among his books are "Rebellion Against the 20th Century Revolution," about American post-war conservatism, and "No, Mr. Prime Minister!" on the experience of the advisor to the Prime Minister.

The February lecture from the cycle Anarchocapitalism will be devoted to so-called market "failures"; or perhaps it would not be appropriate to write "market" failure - indeed, on the basis of them, suboptimal allocation of resources can occur (i.e. outside the Pareto optimum), but I do not consider this so much a property of the market, but rather a property of the world. In my opinion, this is one of the most obvious (unfortunately sanctified by the academic sphere) economic mistakes; however, it is unfortunately so widespread that almost every time I mention it, there is a proponent of it. So I decided to devote a whole lecture to him; I'd love for you to come - especially if you believe in market failure - and argue with me and challenge my arguments.

title: EU fines Intel
desc:
In 2009, the EU fined Intel $1.1 billion for "conditional rebates" and "naked restrictions" (payments to those who do not buy from competitors); Intel sued the EU and won in 2022 because the EU's "conditional rebates" failed to prove a specific impact on competition (and the fine did not specify which part was for "conditional rebates" and which part was for "naked restrictions"). In 2023, the EU demonstrated the effects of "naked restrictions", for which it fined Intel $386 million; but Intel sued the EU for lost interest on the wrongful fine, which had risen to $536 over those 15 years. The entire court case therefore cost taxpayers $150 million - if we do not count the expenses for the European Union authorities, which messed up the decision and subsequently dealt with it for many years.

That story deserves (in addition to our money) Hitler's commentary with subtitles, don't you think?

Four reasons for separating the judiciary from the state!
Like any monopoly maintained by force, the state judiciary provides expensive and poor quality services.
Just as other professions compete in the free market, so can judges. Where there is a demand for justice and dispute resolution, there is also a supply. 
The impartiality of state judges is only illusory. The state pays them and appoints them to positions, so at least they cannot be impartial in disputes with the state. Moreover, instead of finding justice, judges only interpret the intentions of the state to organize social relations.
Only a decentralized judiciary allows each dispute to be judged by someone who does not belong to either party; more information can be found, for example, in the recordings of lectures on polycentric law; you can listen to them here - on the Freeport Channel.

Sometimes you send me interesting texts and videos; and I just came across bans on energy drinks for minors, a ban on HHC or other drugs, and a rejected request for euthanasia. Seemingly quite unrelated topics; however, I see one common denominator in them - the will of the state and the effort to own us.
Self-ownership is one of the cornerstones of libertarianism and anarcho-capitalism; we primarily own ourselves – our body – and subsequently the fruits of our labor. But is it really so? Who ultimately decides what we can and cannot do with our bodies? Unfortunately, the answer won't surprise anyone much; but why?

Václav Szőcs is a libertarian and long-term supporter of the Free Port; at the same time, he is a critic of the ideology of progressivism, which he considers a potential threat, since totalitarianism can be built on it, which I agree with him on.

The April lecture from the cycle Anarchocapitalism will be about different (non)paths to (non)freedom; both on an individual and societal level. We will talk not only about what steps in my opinion lead to freedom (and here I develop a lot over the years, I reevaluate my views - perhaps as a result of a deeper understanding of freedom), but also about which paths do not lead to freedom, or may even cause the opposite of the intended result (here I am fairly constant over time, although I notice certain - rather minor - changes of opinion in this as well). Moreover, it is possible to aim at two seemingly different goals - freedom for oneself as an individual and freedom for society; here the first makes more and more sense to me, but I also perceive an increasing "overlap" of both approaches.

The March lecture from the Anarcho-Capitalism series will be about state licenses and authorizations to do things that we have a natural right to do; nevertheless, the state fit the role of someone who should allow us to do what it has no business doing - even in cases where we do not harm anyone and do not violate anyone's freedom or property. To carry out many activities, we need licenses of various types - whether it is teaching, social work, driving a motor vehicle, treating or burying people, food production, banking services, auctions, tourism or simply "just" a certificate of medical fitness for any profession (including office). The sixth speaker of the "Freeport Conference 2024: Technology yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Jan Romportl with his lecture "How AI has burned into us through ChatGPT".

The ChatGPT system, which was presented to the public by OpenAI at the end of November 2022, achieved several major results. For example: (1) planet-wide ChatGPT fetishism; (2) the emergence of an incredible number of new "AI experts" whining about language models and whose jobs those models will take away; (3) popular influencers, who until recently unboxed, tested and commented on new iPhones and filmed themselves doing so on YouTube, are now unboxing new AI products in the same style and spreading consumer awareness about them to the lay public; (4) alerting an unexpectedly large number of people that there really might be some kind of AI; (5) the strained argumentative gymnastics of AI opponents who rely on the notion that ChatGPT is just a "statistical parrot" that, unlike a human, does not "truly" understand the text; (6) OpenAI suggests that they are indeed starting to approach Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and that we should finally start paying attention. So... So how are we really doing now? What piece is still missing between big language models and AGI? Why is A(G)I one of humanity's main hopes and at the same time a fundamental existential risk? You can look forward to all this in the lecture.

Jan Romportl, founder and former CEO of Dataclair.ai, is now an independent AI consultant and runs his own startup that focuses on solving the problems of today's online world with AI. A PhD holder in Artificial Intelligence and Philosophy, he has over 12 years of university research and teaching in the areas of Artificial Intelligence and Human Machine Interaction. His experience also includes a leading position in the Department of Human-Machine Interaction at the University of West Bohemia in Pilsen and cooperation with the Center for Theoretical Studies of Charles University and the Association for Effective Altruism.

The fifth speaker of the "Free Port Conference 2024: Technology yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Honza Skalický with his lecture "Fraud on the Internet and the digital footprint".

The lecture will deal with the phenomenon of fraud on the Internet, make a brief classification of them and focus on a common type of fraudulent purchase of goods. It analyzes the digital trail they can leave and how it can be used to prosecute fraudsters. The presented situations will be illustrated by examples from practice, and at the end we will also think about the role of the state in the problem being addressed.

Ing. Jan Skalický studied computer technology at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Czech Technical University. He currently works as a head of SW development and a lecturer of programming courses. In addition to positions as a specialist in the development of microcomputer systems, he also worked at the Temelín nuclear power plant. He is the co-author of two books on the subject.

The third speaker of the "2024 Freeport Conference: Technology Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his talk "Fear Against Freedom".

Human history is full of fascinating inventions and innovations that have often changed people's lives and society beyond recognition; of course, most such changes did not come without massive fears about the future - human progress is fringed by fear of the unknown. The older generations have been cursing the younger since time immemorial; many people in virtually every historical epoch feel that the real or metaphorical end of the world is approaching. Nevertheless, we always manage in the end; and not only that, as a company we are constantly developing and improving in the long term. However, fear is immutable; the rulers have long since understood that it can be used to rule and control the masses, so they like to feed it. How can one approach this? Is there anything we can do? And if so, what exactly?

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author; wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. For fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, education, the free market, the economy and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, makes videos and is invited to various programs and panel discussions. Co-creates Freeport; teaches at the free school Ježek without a cage and has been actively cooperating with many libertarian initiatives for a long time.

The video was produced in collaboration with the Libertarian Institute; you can support him here:
https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons for free market legislation!
The Department of State Analysis of the Institute of State and Law of the Academy of Sciences found that in 2010 there were about 1.6 million legal norms in the Czech Republic, and in the long term they are increasing by 55 thousand per year. So today we probably have over two million valid orders, prohibitions, regulations and legislative orders.
Although ignorance of the law is no excuse, there is no one who knows all the laws. Lawyers are also represented by colleagues if they are conducting a dispute outside their field of law. Officials often do not even know the few laws under which they are supposed to work.
Because of the state, we live in a legislative jungle; we have become accustomed to solving all problems with laws that politicians churn out like on a treadmill. The state thus controls our lives more and more, which is a sure way to totalitarianism.

The video was produced in collaboration with the Libertarian Institute; you can support him here:
https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons not to trust the government!
We recognize the propaganda of historical or foreign regimes easily because we are not used to it. In contrast, we tend to ignore the propaganda that we are exposed to all the time.
Propaganda does not belong only to totalitarian dictatorships; all governments – even democratic ones – have a need to shape their citizens in a certain direction.
From an early age, we were all continuously indoctrinated in schools with theses about the necessity of the state, the correctness of democracy or the dysfunctionality of anarchy; the result is the inability of most people to think critically about these topics.
Schools are not the only vehicle for spreading propaganda; the media - especially the public ones - or the ubiquitous signs announcing what the EU has financed, as well as a number of so-called fact-checkers, in addition to information, push us emotions and the "right" view.

The October lecture from the cycle Anarchocapitalism will be about decentralization; this, in my opinion, is very closely related to freedom - after all, it is not for nothing that I describe anarcho-capitalism in four equivalent ways for me: (a) mutual voluntariness, (b) complete demonopolization, (c) absolute decentralization and (d) the principle of subsidiarity and the right to self-determination brought to fruition. Although decentralization tends to be better accepted by people than anarcho-capitalism, it nevertheless raises a number of concerns; these mainly revolve around the impossibility (or considerable complexity) of controlling decentralized systems (compared to centralized systems). What about when "undesirable" enclaves, such as racism, sexism, religious fundamentalism or sectarianism, begin to emerge in a decentralized society? You can learn that - and much more - at the lecture.

In September, Markéta Čermáková will lecture on anarcho-capitalism; he will talk about the fact that the state guarantees children the right to education by imposing it on them as an obligation. The state promises to take into account the educational needs of the individual, mutual respect and tolerance, tolerance of opinions, solidarity and dignity of all participants in education. Among other things, it imposes on educators the obligation to create a positive and safe climate in the school environment and to support its development through their approach to education and training. Does that sound good to you? To Marquette (apart from that duty) yes. Does this sound like a description of most mainstream schools? Unfortunately not. We will look at the ways in which legislation and school practice most often differ. And also to the main thing - why education, as it is set up, does not take into account the real needs of children, and how else (and why) children can be educated happily and effectively.

--------
Four reasons why the state should not restrict freedom of speech!
All communication platform rules should be determined by their owners; including any restrictions. State intervention in any direction contradicts property rights.
If we ban the public presentation of some opinions, they will not disappear from society anyway; on the contrary, it will be much more difficult to oppose them than if we let them be heard.
I believe in finding the truth through dialogue. If we suppress criticism of a position, we limit the possibility of its constant review and possible reevaluation.
Words have great power to do much harm; however, they have exactly the same power in defense against such damage. Let us fight against word with word, against sword with sword.

--------
The video was produced in collaboration with the Libertarian Institute; you can support him here:
https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons why the state does not need to build roads!
People want to be transported; and where there is demand, there is also supply in the free market.
The state has no additional resources available to it beyond those it collects from taxpayers. To give an idea: No company in the Czech Republic has such profits as the state earns from motorists after accounting for all costs. 
Notoriously known corruption - connected precisely with the construction of the road network - is, in principle, only possible where someone makes decisions about other people's finances - just like the state about taxpayers' money.
The private investor is motivated to manage and operate roads to the satisfaction of their users; not according to current – often ideological – political demand.

Whether it is a comparison with communism as a "nice theory", the homo economicus model, the demand for a "new anarcho-capitalist man" and a change in human nature, or the idea that evolution shows the dysfunctionality of an establishment that has not historically prevailed, it seems to me that many - although certainly not all - efforts to refute (or perhaps overthrow) anarcho-capitalism are burdened by ignorance of the topic. I would like to elaborate on some of them; as part of this, I also intend to outline realistically functional (albeit slow) paths to freedom (and eventually a stateless society). I will be very happy for your questions, polemics and this time more than ever for comments and suggestions.
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/decentrala/

The April lecture from the Anarchocapitalism cycle will be devoted to how the state harms the poor; and this despite the fact that as part of his propaganda he constantly convinces everyone of the opposite. Many people believe that in a world without the state, it would be the poor today who would be the ones to suffer; however, in my opinion, this is a big illusion created by the state in order to create fear and thereby justify its existence. Even if the state is redistributing to help some of the poor - which is very easy to see - there are plenty of other (really strong) state influences that clearly harm the poor - which is much harder to see. Let's focus on them and look - like Frédéric Bastiat - at what (at least at first glance) is not visible.

The March lecture from the Anarcho-Capitalism cycle will be about the "war mentality"; about a vision of the world in which all people belong either to the "us" category (that is, the good, righteous, decent and kind-hearted ones with pure intentions and striving for a good world), or to the "them" category (that is, the bad, vile, bad and evil sons with dark intentions and an effort to do harm). The third speaker of the "2023 Freeport Conference: Drugs and Guns Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his talk "Time of Prohibitions".

What happens when we ban something? Regardless of the reasons or the meaningfulness of such a ban, most people have a need to believe that the ban in question is meaningful; without knowing anything about the given issue, they can retroactively "invent" why this or that was forbidden and what would "certainly happen" if it was not forbidden. There's just one catch - very often it's simply not true; however, this does not prevent states from exploiting this ignorance (and fear) in enforcing bans. Drugs and guns used to be common "everyday" items a hundred years ago; until quite recently they were stigmatized and banned - yet it seems that only without them can our civilization function. It's interesting that a lot of people who have learned the futility of drug or gun bans are vehemently pushing for the regulation of the other... Why?

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author; wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. For fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, education, the free market, the economy and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, makes videos and is invited to various programs and panel discussions. Together with his wife Teresa, he forms the Free Harbor; teaches at the independent school Hedgehog without a cage; he heads the Czech and Slovak Institute of Ludwig von Mises, of which he is a co-founder; he belongs to the board of the Freedom of Learning association and has been actively cooperating with many libertarian initiatives for a long time. We all grew up in a society that treats drugs as a phenomenon of the modern age, for which it is a scarecrow, and as responsible individuals we should fight against it by all means. From history, we may vaguely remember the hippie movement or the development of meth-cooking plants in socialist Czechoslovakia, but otherwise we consider the use of addictive substances by the lay public to be relevant especially for the present. The December lecture from the Anarchocapitalism cycle will be devoted to the regulatory principles of anarchocapitalism; despite popular belief among people who have heard little of anarcho-capitalism, anarchy does not mean the absence of rules, but only the absence of (forced and involuntary) rulers. However, people need - and therefore demand - rules for their daily lives, therefore they create them also on a voluntary basis; however, unlike central planners, the free market has the ability to flexibly create, change, and cancel these rules according to the momentary needs of its participants. Four reasons why states and politicians always lose in the fight against corruption!
Space for corruption arises wherever someone makes decisions about other people's money. And deciding on foreign money is the very essence of the state.
Unfortunately, every control authority that should fight and combat corruption is also corruptible in principle. There is no reason why he shouldn't be; nor a way to ensure it.
In principle, incorruptible are those who manage their own – not other people's – money and property; bribing them then means nothing more than making a deal with them.
The only truly effective way to fight corruption is to eliminate public budgets and leave the money in the hands of those who earned it.

For several years now, every September lecture from the Anarchocapitalism series has been about education or children. However, we have not yet covered children's rights in anarcho-capitalism, as there is (surprisingly) not much demand for this topic; however, the time has slowly matured, so we will talk about children in a stateless society. Does self-ownership apply to them? Who has the authority to make decisions for them on issues they do not (yet) understand? Who will - as weaker individuals - protect them? What if someone abuses children? Can something be done about it even without the state? Can a child enter into contracts? And what if she decides to leave her parents and go her own way? What will a society look like without banning child labor? If you are interested in the answers to these and other questions, come and listen to the lecture; and possibly ask about anything yourself.

Radim Passer entered the Guinness Book of Records by driving over 400 km/h on a German autobahn in his Bugatti; in fact, he did it twice, with Bugatti congratulating him for it in 2015 and disavowing it in 2022. Why? What has changed?
How do people's reactions to this event relate to reactions to the anti-smoking law, drug and gun bans, or perhaps the obligation to handcuff yourself behind the wheel or not drink in canoes? I believe that they are all heavily influenced by the degree of understanding of others' subjective preferences; and I am convinced that if they were not, we would live in a better society.

--------
Four reasons why housing is so expensive!
Construction is such an extremely over-regulated industry that only entities large enough to dedicate enough people to just deal with the red tape can operate in it. This limits competition and raises prices.
Due to state regulations, construction procedures are extremely long, which increases costs. It is not built when the owner needs it, but when officials and politicians allow it. The offer then hardly responds to the demand.
The state's monetary policy consists in the permanent devaluation of the currency. Because of the state, money thus lost the ability to store value in the long term; people then store this in real estate, among other things, which increases their prices.
In addition to Czech regulations, European ones also affect us; of these, especially green policy requirements (for example, energy labels and the like) increase the price of housing.

Four reasons for the separation of healthcare from the state!
State socialist health care is killing people as a result of misallocation of resources; overworked, tired medical professionals or long waiting times for CT, MRI and other examinations can mean the difference between life and death.
Fees for true market health insurance would be based not on salary but on actual risks; people would thus be financially motivated to lead a healthy lifestyle.
During a pandemic, health insurance companies would be motivated to set up anti-epidemic measures for their policyholders as efficiently as possible, because every sick person costs them money; not like politicians who bear no material responsibility for their decisions.
The state prevents doctors and patients from having mutually voluntary relationships; some then get angry at others without realizing that the real problem is in the legislation and the setting of the entire system.

--------
Four reasons why the state poses a great risk to our privacy!
Personal data protection has finally become a societal issue; people began to rightly ask what data private companies collect about them and what they do with it. Unfortunately, the state is completely neglected in similar considerations.
At the same time, we do not even have to give our data to private companies; on the other hand, the state assigns us a birth number at birth and then collects sensitive data about us without consent, from health documentation to records of economic activities.
We have to report a lot of sensitive data to the state under the threat of sanctions. We can only minimally influence the way the state will deal with them - and who will be able to abuse them.
If there is a change of political regime, all state data will remain; therefore, we give them not only to the current government, but also to all future ones. The Jews in Nazi Germany also acknowledged their origin to a government other than the one that exterminated them en masse.

Four reasons not to resign from responsibility for your life!
Freedom and responsibility are two sides of the same coin; a free man bears the consequences of his decisions, from which he constantly learns.
A state that seeks to babysit its citizens absolves them of responsibility for their lives; those concerned then lose not only their freedom of choice, but also the opportunity to learn from mistakes and the ability to make fundamental decisions.
In a society where the state has created a lot of irresponsible people, there is a growing demand for more state intervention; as a result of these, even more irresponsible people are born, who call for even stricter regulations and so on and on.
If people get used to making decisions for themselves and facing various risks, sooner or later the state will end up in the hands of someone who will abuse it against them.

The fifth speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2022: Money yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Mojmír Hampl with his lecture "Elastic money - the essence of the current monetary system".

It is surprising that we all use the monetary system on a daily basis, but often even the most educated people have only a vague or even zero idea of its nature and functioning. In the lecture, we will focus on how the current elastic money system is different from fixed money systems and explain how and where money is created and destroyed.

Mojmír Hampl is a Czech economist, banker and columnist with degrees from the University of Economics in Prague and the University of Surrey in Great Britain. He devoted most of his professional life to date to the Czech National Bank (ČNB), where he joined as an analyst after defending his diploma thesis with the then Vice-Governor of the CNB, Pavel Kysilka.
After a four-year break, when he worked as an economist at Česká spořitelna and later as a member of the management of the Czech Consolidation Agency, he returned to the CNB in 2006 when he was appointed to its banking board. Between 2008 and 2018, he held the position of Deputy Governor of the CNB. Throughout his life, he repeatedly returns to the topic of money, currencies and central banks in his works. This is also why he is known for his very sharp views on the subject of the euro and also European integration. He has published more than three hundred popular and professional articles in various areas of his broad interest - from macroeconomics, through economic history to contributions on the topic of cryptocurrencies. He lectured in many places around the world, especially on monetary policy and central banking.

The third speaker of the "2022 Freeport Conference: Money Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "The Internet of Ancient Times".

I sometimes refer to money in my lectures as the "Ancient Internet"; it is a wonderful means of communication between people, which in addition to information also conveys motivation. In my opinion, this is one of the most important inventions of mankind; it allows us to efficiently allocate resources and send important signals to people whose existence we have no idea, but with whom we can still cooperate and coordinate our wealth-creating efforts through a system of prices. This way of communication is going great until states start disrupting it when they want to "aid and protect" their citizens; most people - politicians included - do not know or understand this invaluable function of money, so they will not even see the consequences of its (partial) paralysis.

Urza is the author of the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism and more than a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media. He not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, education, the market, the economy and the role of the state in society for more than ten years, but also lectures (for example, as part of the series Anarchocapitalismus in Parallel Polis and in (de)Central, but also in schools and at many conferences), makes videos and accepts invitations to various programs or panel discussions where he defends the freedom of the individual.

Account number: 2201359764/2010; variable symbol: 6
--------
The video was produced in collaboration with the Libertarian Institute; you can support him here:
https://www.libertarianskyinstitut.cz/jak-nas-podporit/
--------
Four reasons why to make free market decisions about recycling!
It makes sense to recycle precisely when the resources needed for recycling are less scarce than the resources needed to obtain new raw materials and process old waste.
The rarity of goods on the free market is reflected in their prices. The variant that consumes less rare goods is thus also cheaper. Recycling is therefore more gentle in an undistorted free market precisely when it pays off economically.
Otherwise, recycling is nothing more than a waste of human or natural resources. Depending on the technology used, recycling may consume too much energy, etc.
Artificial state support for recycling leads to a distortion of the market, as a result of which it can be worthwhile to recycle even where it means waste instead of frugality.

Four Reasons Why Central Planning Doesn't Work!
We live in a world of limited resources, where the fulfillment of one wish means that the wish of another cannot be fulfilled. And since no one knows the needs of others better than themselves, each central planner wastes public resources to implement less needed projects at the expense of more needed ones.
The information needed to produce anything is naturally decentralized in society due to the division of labor. The central planner has only limited and distorted access to them; therefore it is woefully inefficient.
In the free market, millions of entrepreneurs are simultaneously trying to do things as best they can by many different methods; the best will naturally take over and expand, the rest will disappear along with failing businesses. In central planning, there is no room for testing so many different approaches and solutions at the same time.
People working for themselves have incomparably more motivation to do good work than those in a socialist economy where "he who does not rob the state robs the family".

Four reasons for separating money from the state!
Money is one of the most amazing inventions of mankind; prices are used to transmit information about the rarity of goods between sellers and buyers around the world. Any artificial intervention in this system distorts information and sends false signals to all market participants, causing a waste of resources.
Interventions by central banks in the economy cause business cycles. Before the existence of central banking, economic crises used to have specific causes - for example, natural disasters, lack of crops and the like; due to interventions by central banks in interest rates, crises occur even without external causes.
Artificial inflation causes injustice because it takes away the value of savings, which is shared between banks and people with access to cheap credit. It makes it impossible to save money effectively and forces even those who do not want to undertake the investment risk.
If the state has power over money, it can at any time decide to devalue everyone's savings for its own benefit; this is how governments typically finance, for example, arming for wars, paying off excessive debts or other large expenditures.

Four reasons why the state helps the rich at the expense of the poor!
Big companies can influence politicians and thus legislation. State regulations then effectively eliminate competition from smaller companies that do not have the means to meet often unnecessary standards and legal norms. 
Even a law adopted in good faith without corruption will rather be prepared with regard to processes in large companies, which are known to politicians and officials. In addition, corporations have entire departments of lawyers, accountants, and other personnel who can deal with regulations; in a small company, everyone is dedicated to the business itself.
Labor market regulations – such as the minimum wage – harm the least qualified, who then become unemployable, as the value of their work may not exceed the state-enforced minimum cost of their employment. Such people go into the gray area and live on social benefits. 
All state requirements for the minimum quality of services or goods make it impossible to sell products that are low-quality but extremely cheap. This makes life easier for the rich who wouldn't buy them anyway; however, the state deprives the poor of the opportunity to satisfy their needs at least somehow.

Four reasons for separating education from the state!
Education is monopolized by the state. He also decides on the conditions for the establishment and operation of private schools. Educating children in a way not approved by the Ministry is not legal even if it is the world's long-term successful learning methods. Parents with a different view on education are threatened with having their children taken away and imprisoned.
Like any monopoly, the state also provides expensive and low-quality services in education. Tabled teacher salaries discourage the able and attract the less able. The education provided by the state does not reflect the real needs of children - many important things are missing and a lot of unnecessary things remain. 
Even before reading, writing and arithmetic, a child learns to obey the authority assigned to him at school. It is difficult for him to start establishing equal relationships when he spends the entire educational process in a subordinate role. The logical consequence is a society full of conforming individuals always ready to submit to dictates and pressure from the outside.
Centralized education is used by states to indoctrinate young children. Each generation learns from a young age about the advantages of the regime it lives in and the disadvantages of other regimes. This effectively prevents critical thinking and constructive debate about the social order.

The first lecture in the new school year will traditionally be about education, i.e. the formal state-monopolized education system and its potential alternatives. For what reason must education be under the control of the state? Why can't we educate ourselves without the supervision of officials and the permission of the ministry? Couldn't education be mutually voluntary? Or must they be mandatory? And wouldn't compulsory education be better than compulsory schooling? How freely can we learn under the current legislation? What is still possible and what is already over the edge?
You can listen to and discuss all this not only with Urza, but also with Gabriela Ježková. This native of Brno has been dedicated to children and education basically her whole life; a few years ago, she founded the now legendary school Ježek bez klece - one of the freest elementary schools in the Czech Republic.

title: A spiritual debate about freedom at the self-reliance festival
desc:
I gladly accepted the invitation to the Soběsta(te)čnosti festival organized by the Sklenářky community; and I must say that I really liked it there.
This is a recording from the circle of elders, in which we discussed the inner and outer freedom of the individual as well as society and other "higher" entities. I warn viewers in advance that this is not a classic debate, as you are used to from the Freeport Channel - this one is much more spiritual and esoteric. So don't expect a battle of logical arguments; it was much more a matter of feeling, which was the declared goal from the very beginning. Personally, such a format has greatly enriched me, because I try to be more in touch with my emotions, which such a "circle" definitely helps. I will be happy if you write in the comments what you think about it, or if and how this video enriched you. Personally, I would probably look down on a similar conversation before; but I am glad for myself that it is no longer the case today. What do you think?

--------
Four reasons to save for (your entire) retirement!
The continuous pension system is a plane - a pyramid scheme. Although the state forces us to contribute huge amounts of money to the system, what we get back from it is in the stars. The plane only works when new participants continue to enter the system and pay off the older ones.
Although politicians see that the pension system is collapsing, and even talk about it lately, they have no reason to do anything about it. They are elected for four years, so they have no reason to take unpopular measures to solve a problem, the consequences of which will be felt when they themselves are secured in political retirement.
The state is a lousy landlord; spends and gets more and more in debt. No one asks if they will go into debt anymore; we only deal with how much. A deficit in "mere" tens of billions is considered a success. Do you really believe that such an institution will take care of you in your old age better than you yourself?
We have no guarantees. When the money runs out, politicians will simply blame the incompetence of previous politicians. Pensions don't just have to be ridiculously small; the retirement limit can also be moved arbitrarily. Therefore, do not rely on the state and try to secure the entire pension yourself.

--------
Four reasons why the state should not protect us!
Whenever the state protects us from any danger, it assumes part of the responsibility for our life. In that area, we have less freedom, which politicians take away from us through laws. The more "protected" we are, the less we make decisions about our lives.
The less we make decisions about our lives and the more the state protects us, the less we are able to take care of ourselves. Instead of ourselves, we rely on laws, politicians, government and government assistance. We are trying to solve a new problem with a new claim on the state. We are becoming dependent on the state.
The more people depend on the state, the more likely we will pass this dependence on to our children and future generations. Instead of self-confident and responsible individuals, society will be made up of people who are "entitled" to state aid.
If society is made up of people who "entitle" to state aid, it will cause a spiral of constant state growth. We will be "protected" even where we don't need or want it. Under the guise of protecting us, politicians will abuse their power and impose their ideas on how we should live.

desc:

--------

--------
Four reasons to remember opportunity cost!
We live in a world of limited resources. So anything we do carries with it what is called an opportunity cost—that is, whatever we gave up in favor of what we did. It cost us at least time, but often something extra.
If we go to the movies instead of the gym, we sacrifice the opportunity to improve our fitness for the opportunity to watch a movie. And in exactly the same way, even nobler goals - for example, protecting the environment - are always realized at the expense of something - for example, treating the sick.
Every law, every regulation, every regulation, every investment, simply any state intervention has a price – not only money paid in taxes, but also unproduced goods, unprovided services, unrealized projects, jobs that will not be created, our time and the possibility of choice.
Opportunity costs must always be taken into account, i.e. when evaluating any state agenda - new or existing. The benefit of people spending their own money according to their preferences cannot be replaced by any state agenda.

Four Reasons Why We Need Market Prices!
Prices are a brilliant and irreplaceable tool to convey information. If something is in short supply, the price rises, which informs and motivates all market participants. The one who directs resources to the production of scarce goods or invents a substitute for them will earn. In the event of a surplus, the price falls again and resources are shifted elsewhere.
Prices also determine consumer behavior. Higher prices motivate consumers to save on scarce goods, or to replace them with something else - cheaper and therefore less rare. This saves not only human labor but also natural resources.
We influence the money in the market what we are really interested in. This leads to a better allocation of resources than when the state decides based on the will of the voters. Through elections, everyone tries to assert their abstract preferences at the expense of others, and thus projects are created that people would not spend their own money on.
In a truly free and free market undistorted by the state, those who can best satisfy the needs of the people who willingly pay for it will become the richest. Not those who are fine with politicians and officials making decisions about other people's money.

Four Reasons Why Democracy Is Not As Good As They Tell You!
Even a democratic majority can be wrong. In addition, he decides on things that everyone can decide in his own way. We don't need a one-size-fits-all solution. You make the best decisions about your affairs and money yourself, because you know your needs better than others.
Under the communists, the leading role of the Communist Party was enshrined in the constitution, today we have compulsory democracy. However, democracy without questioning and without restrictions can easily become totalitarianism, i.e. a system affecting all areas of people's lives. There are more and more things that we would like differently than they are democratically decided.
Democracy breaks up society because it turns people into rivals. If we could live our own lives, we wouldn't have to mind people with different values. However, when they can impose their views on us through elections, they are dangerous for us. Instead of tolerance and cooperation, we compete for a share of the collected money; about what we can and can't do.
We are not prospering as we could because of democracy. For more and more people, using the neighbor's state for part of their earnings is more attractive than working as hard as they do.  Therefore, there are more and more "entitled" ones, while those who create values are decreasing.

Although most people imagine something under the term "monopoly" - and even suspect that it is something harmful; however, few distinguish between a true monopoly and a dominant market player, but what's worse - the biggest, most harmful, most violent and most widespread monopoly is completely neglected and ignored. Yes, this is a state that can afford everything that no one else could afford. How is that? Well, by consistently abusing its monopoly position in education, it constantly indoctrinates everyone with its propaganda from the earliest age; people are then willing to view the state in a completely different way than all other subjects.
Through the analysis of the monopoly position of the state, the attitudes of anarcho-capitalists can also be clearly described. Contrary to popular belief, they do not want a world without the services that states provide; in fact, they only seek to de-monopolize the state and enable competition.

There are a number of barriers and pitfalls in communication with socialists and generally everyone from the opposite side of the opinion spectrum; however, many of them are more communicative in nature than fundamental. Adam Růžička's lecture for the "Free Harbor Conference 2020: Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow" was entitled "Creeping social tyranny and the importance of freedom of speech".

Under the term tyranny, we usually imagine the violent dictate of a powerful individual or group that oppresses the rest. However, thinkers have long pointed out that tyranny can also manifest itself on a social level, in ways that are harder to define, but all the more insidious, because they are not clearly visible, but often have a comparable influence on the lives of individuals as despotic governments. This threat to free societies was described by John Stuart Mill in his famous essay On Freedom, and Václav Havel also touched on it in The Power of the Powerless when he spoke of social "self-totality". The lecture will present the basic theses of the issue of social freedom and connect them with recent psychological research in the context of the current challenges of democratic societies (e.g. social media, opinion bubbles, the phenomenon of divided societies, etc.).

After studying psychology at Masaryk University, Adam Růžička, MSc. MRes. at University College London, where he worked for several years as a researcher in the field of cognitive neuroscience and researched the brain with a focus on human speech. He currently works as the director of the H21 Institute in Prague, which focuses on collective decision-making, electoral systems, civic participation and the issue of a divided society.

The next speaker at the "Freeport Conference 2020: Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Jan Zugar with his lecture "North Korea - a country much more open than we perceive it".

There is perhaps no country more emotionally closed to the outside world than the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. In 1950-53, a war took place here, during which the country was divided into southern and northern parts due to the efforts of the north, which sought, with the support of China and the Soviet Union, to unite the entire country under the red flag. This failed thanks to the intervention of UN troops, and so after a three-year conflict, Korea was divided into these two parts by the 38th parallel. While South Korea is a developing country that is moving in the same direction as comparable eastern states, North Korea is closed, an information embargo is imposed on the media of the surrounding countries, access to the Internet, which is also internal only to the DPRK, is almost impossible and the harsh dictatorship of the Communist Party and the Kim clan rules here. It is very rare to get to this country as part of diplomatic trips or a study stay, which Jan Zugar was able to do.

Any historian will tell you how historical totalities worked. But how to recognize future totalitarian ideologies and how to survive them? What is the fundamental difference between totalitarianism and dictatorship? Can totality arise only through the state, or are there real "grassroots" totalities from secret groups of fanatics?

The second speaker of the "2020 Freeport Conference: Totality Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "The Different Faces of Evil or Recognize Totality".

Although everyone can probably agree that they don't want to live in totalitarianism, for some reason totalitarian regimes are an inherent part of our history; and not only long past, but also quite recent, in short, they keep coming again and again. How is this possible, you ask, when almost everyone rejects totalitarianism? Well, few people offer it to people directly; totalitarian regimes typically come under the guise of promises of safety, prosperity, well-being, and often even freedom. Unfortunately, history shows that most people do not recognize totalitarianism until it is too late. And because Urza does not want (perhaps not only) to repeat this history, during this lecture he will try to teach you to recognize the arrival of totalitarian regimes while there is still time.

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author; wrote about a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. For more than ten years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, the free market, the economy and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, makes videos and is invited to various programs and panel discussions. Together with his wife Teresa, he forms the Free Harbor; he heads the Czech and Slovak Institute of Ludwig von Mises, of which he is a co-founder; belongs to the board of the Freedom of Learning association and actively cooperates with many libertarian initiatives.
